questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has sudden painless loss of vision in her right eye on waking. Acuity is hand movements only. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula.
questions.lead: What is the most important condition to exclude urgently?
questions.explanation: This is central retinal artery occlusion — a stroke of the eye. In anyone over 50 you must exclude giant cell arteritis, because the fellow eye can be lost within days and high-dose corticosteroids are started on clinical suspicion, without waiting for ESR, CRP or temporal artery biopsy. Ask about headache, jaw claudication and scalp tenderness. Also investigate the embolic source — carotids and cardiac.
questions.point: Sudden painless vision loss over 50 requires urgent exclusion of giant cell arteritis, with steroids started on suspicion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a severely painful red right eye, headache, nausea and vomiting. She reports haloes around lights. The cornea is hazy, the pupil is mid-dilated and fixed, and the globe feels hard.
questions.explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — the combination of a fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, hard globe and haloes is characteristic. The nausea and vomiting are the trap: patients are sometimes worked up for an abdominal or neurological cause while the eye goes unexamined. Treat urgently with pressure-lowering agents, acetazolamide and pilocarpine, then laser peripheral iridotomy to BOTH eyes, since the fellow eye is anatomically at risk.
questions.point: Acute angle-closure glaucoma gives a fixed mid-dilated pupil with a hard globe, and often presents with vomiting.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old contact lens wearer has a painful red left eye with photophobia and blurred vision for two days. There is a white corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Same-day ophthalmology referral for corneal scrape and intensive topical antibiotics
Eye patching and review in one week
Topical chloramphenicol and review in 5 days
questions.explanation: A contact lens wearer with a red painful eye has microbial keratitis until proven otherwise — including Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba. This is sight-threatening and needs same-day referral for scrape and intensive fortified topical antibiotics. Do not patch (it incubates infection) and do not give topical steroid, which worsens infection and risks corneal melt.
questions.point: A contact lens wearer with a red painful eye has microbial keratitis until proven otherwise and needs same-day referral.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis has a painful red right eye with photophobia. The redness is most marked around the limbus. The pupil is small and irregular. Vision is mildly reduced.
questions.lead: What is the diagnosis and its significance?
options: Anterior uveitis; associated with HLA-B27 conditions
questions.explanation: Circumciliary (limbal) flush with a small irregular pupil from posterior synechiae is anterior uveitis. The systemic link is what makes it examinable: HLA-B27 conditions — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, IBD, psoriatic arthritis — plus sarcoidosis, TB and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Treatment is topical corticosteroid plus a cycloplegic, which relieves ciliary spasm and prevents further synechiae.
questions.point: Anterior uveitis causes circumciliary flush with a small irregular pupil and is associated with HLA-B27 conditions.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man reports that straight lines on his bathroom tiles now appear wavy, and he has a grey patch in his central vision that developed over two weeks. Peripheral vision is unaffected.
options: Progression of dry age-related macular degeneration
Conversion to wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration
questions.explanation: Metamorphopsia — straight lines appearing wavy — with rapid central loss is the hallmark of conversion to wet AMD. This matters because it is treatable and urgent: intravitreal anti-VEGF preserves vision, and delay costs it. Dry AMD progresses slowly over years without distortion. Patients monitor with an Amsler grid and are told to present immediately if it changes. Peripheral vision is preserved in AMD, which distinguishes it from glaucoma.
questions.point: Metamorphopsia with rapid central vision loss indicates conversion to wet AMD and needs urgent anti-VEGF.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an eye examination. Fundoscopy shows microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates and several cotton wool spots, but no new vessels.
questions.lead: How is this classified and what is the main threat to his vision?
questions.explanation: New vessels are absent, so this is non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. The commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes is diabetic maculopathy — macular oedema or exudates threatening the fovea — and crucially it can occur at any retinopathy stage, including this one. Cotton wool spots are nerve fibre layer infarcts indicating ischaemia. Treat maculopathy with anti-VEGF; panretinal photocoagulation is for proliferative disease.
questions.point: Diabetic maculopathy is the commonest cause of vision loss in diabetes and can occur at any stage of retinopathy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has blurred vision in her left eye developing over three days, with pain on eye movement. Acuity is 6/24 on the left and 6/6 on the right. Colour vision is markedly reduced on the left. There is a left relative afferent pupillary defect. The optic disc appears normal.
questions.lead: How should the normal-looking disc be interpreted?
options: It is consistent with retrobulbar optic neuritis
It indicates a functional visual disorder
questions.explanation: A normal disc is entirely compatible with retrobulbar optic neuritis — the classic phrase is that the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing, because the inflammation is behind the globe. The RAPD and disproportionate colour desaturation localise the lesion to the optic nerve regardless of disc appearance. Strongly associated with multiple sclerosis; IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery but does not change final acuity, and oral prednisolone alone is avoided.
questions.point: Retrobulbar optic neuritis presents with a normal-looking optic disc, so a normal fundus does not exclude it.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is found on screening to have an intraocular pressure of 26 mmHg, a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 with inferior notching, and an arcuate scotoma on perimetry. He has no symptoms.
options: Observation alone as he is asymptomatic
questions.explanation: Primary open-angle glaucoma — asymptomatic until advanced, because peripheral field is lost first while central acuity is preserved. Topical prostaglandin analogue (latanoprost) is first-line. Note the side effects worth knowing: iris darkening, eyelash growth and periorbital fat atrophy. Laser peripheral iridotomy treats angle-CLOSURE, not open-angle, and is the distractor. Absence of symptoms is not a reason to observe — the field loss is irreversible.
questions.point: Topical prostaglandin analogues are first-line for primary open-angle glaucoma; iridotomy is for angle-closure.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has headaches worse on lying flat and transient episodes of visual greying lasting seconds. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally. MRI brain and venography are normal; CSF opening pressure is 31 cmH2O with normal constituents.
questions.lead: Which assessment is most important for monitoring her vision?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The threat is permanent visual loss, and the visual FIELDS deteriorate first while central acuity is preserved until very late — so normal 6/6 vision is falsely reassuring and acuity is a poor monitor. Formal perimetry is the required assessment. Transient visual obscurations with papilloedema indicate the nerve is already threatened. Management: weight loss, acetazolamide, and surgical options if vision deteriorates.
questions.point: In idiopathic intracranial hypertension the visual fields are monitored, because central acuity is preserved until late.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old neonate has bilateral purulent eye discharge with marked lid swelling. The mother had no antenatal care.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure — this is normal neonatal stickiness
Topical chloramphenicol and review in 48 hours
Urgent assessment with swabs and systemic antibiotics for possible gonococcal infection
questions.explanation: Ophthalmia neonatorum presenting in the first days with copious purulent discharge suggests Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which can perforate the cornea within hours and cause blindness. It requires urgent assessment, swabs including PCR, and SYSTEMIC antibiotics — topical alone is inadequate. Chlamydia typically presents later, around days 5-14. Both are notifiable and require maternal and partner treatment.
questions.point: Purulent neonatal conjunctivitis in the first days of life suggests gonococcal infection and needs systemic antibiotics urgently.
